h: From the Hill family to Historic Royal Palaces
p: The house was built in the eighteenth century for the Hill family, later the Marquesses of Downshire, who gave the village its name. In 1925 it was bought by the government to be the home of the Governor of Northern Ireland, and after that post was abolished in the early 1970s it became the official residence of the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland as well as a royal residence. Since 2014 it has been cared for by Historic Royal Palaces, the same charity behind the Tower of London and Hampton Court.
That background is why the place feels like a working house rather than a frozen museum. Real meetings, receptions and royal visits still happen here.

Plan on at least half a day so you're not rushing the gardens after the tour. If you've got kids with you, set them a challenge to find the Temple and the Grotto, which turns a garden walk into a treasure hunt.

In the village, Hillsborough Fort is a seventeenth-century artillery fort sitting on the edge of Hillsborough Forest Park, which has a big lake with a walking path round it, ideal for a gentle loop after lunch. Lisburn is a few miles up the road, and Belfast is within easy reach if you're basing yourself in the city.
